questions.q: By default, where does a container's stdout/stderr output go?
options: Into that container's logs, captured by Docker's default json-file logging driver
It is discarded unless the --verbose flag is passed to docker run
Directly to the host's /var/log/syslog file
Nowhere, unless you explicitly configure a logging driver first
questions.explain: Docker captures stdout/stderr automatically using the json-file driver unless a different logging driver is configured.

questions.q: What's a key risk of the default json-file logging driver if max-size and max-file are never set?
options: It only logs messages at the error level
The container is automatically removed once logs reach 1 GB
It refuses to log anything after 24 hours
Logs can grow unbounded and fill up host disk over time
questions.explain: Without size/rotation limits, json-file keeps appending indefinitely, which can eventually exhaust disk space on the host.

options: Limits the container to logging only 50 more lines going forward
Follows new log output in real time, starting from the last 50 lines of history
Deletes all but the 50 most recent log lines
Shows only the first 50 lines ever logged, then exits immediately
questions.explain: -f follows the log stream live, while --tail 50 seeds the initial output with the most recent 50 lines instead of the full history.

questions.q: What does docker stats show that directly relates back to the resource limits set in Lesson 27?
options: The container's full build history
Live CPU and memory usage alongside the configured MEM USAGE / LIMIT, so you can compare usage to the cap you set
The container's exposed ports
The container's restart policy
questions.explain: docker stats displays current resource usage next to the configured limit, letting you see how close a container is to the --memory/--cpus ceiling from Lesson 27.

questions.q: Why would Northbridge want to centralize logs from containers across multiple hosts instead of just running docker logs on each one?
options: It automatically fixes any bugs found in the logs
Checking logs host-by-host doesn't scale once an application spans more than one machine -- a central aggregator gives one searchable place across all of them
Centralizing logs is required before docker stats will run
docker logs only works for exactly one container, ever, on any host
questions.explain: Once a stack spans multiple hosts, manually checking logs on each one becomes impractical -- centralizing logs gives one place to search across the whole stack.
